newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: No Swiss gold reserve sales before 1999 - SNB.
newsitem.headline: No Swiss gold reserve sales before 1999 - SNB.

text.p: Switzerland will not be able to start selling gold before 1999 to finance a planned human rights foundation and other national projects, the Swiss National Bank (SNB) and Swiss commercial bankers said on Wednesday.
They dismissed as outlandish recent speculation in London bullion markets that the central bank might already be quietly unloading gold through Swiss commercial banks.
"This is not even possible. The whole issue of gold is linked first to the constitution and second to a number of laws based on the constitution," SNB spokesman Werner Abegg said.
"Constitutionally and legally the Swiss National Bank has not been able to sell or buy gold since the early 1970s."

The Swiss government proposed last week creating a seven billion Swiss franc humanitarian foundation that would sell revalued official gold reserves over 10 years to raise money for victims of poverty, human rights abuses and the Holocaust.
The SNB could raise 14 billion francs by valuing its 2,600 tonnes of reserves at around 60 percent of market prices rather than at the current fixed legal parity of 4,595 francs per kilo.
The plan must still win legislative approval and faces a referendum likely to be held in 1998.
Abegg said the issue of gold sales arose because parliament was about to review the whole complex of laws governing the handling of Swiss gold reserves in any event.

"That is the only reason we will be standing -- probably in two years if everything goes very fast -- before the question of what will happen with the gain from revaluation. Before that it is entirely impossible for the SNB to transact in gold."

London dealers say Swiss banks last week actively bought put options around $325 and granted calls in what some suspected could reflect official sales. One senior Swiss banker said he was unfamiliar with banks' exact option trading details, but dismissed the idea that official sales had already started.

"This is complete nonsense. Entire laws and the constitution have to be changed. The Swiss National Bank will not be able to sell gold before 1999," he said, although he added it would be easier to change the law to allow gold lending in the meantime.

"A lot of hedging is being done because although the gold price is higher for technical reasons, the trend is down," another Swiss bank gold specialist said. He ruled out the possibility that the SNB was already in the market.
The SNB's Abegg said the gold sales plan was justified because of the country's large reserves.

"We have per capita by far the largest gold reserves in the world. You can have reserves, but you can have too many reserves," he said, noting the U.S. and Germany were the only Group of 10 countries with larger gold holdings.

Asked if last week's surprise announcement meant Switzerland would ease its historic resistance to gold sales by the International Monetary Fund, Abegg said, "That is a question that must be analysed further too.

"But let's make this very positive here. Even if Switzerland succeeds in transferring part of its gold reserves to such a foundation and then has less reserves, its overall reserve position is still an extremely comfortable reserve position."
The gold sales plan, brainchild of SNB Chairman Hans Meyer, reflects a broader debate about gold now that its traditional role as a hedge against inflation is fading.

"Everone agrees today that for currency developments, even for interest rates, gold is probably not an issue any more," Abegg said, although he added no one could exclude the possibility that gold would one day regain its past importance.
The fact that the Swiss plan to revalue gold at only 60 percent of market value also reflects a conservative approach.
